name: Comply Do
tagline: Compliance software for tracking controls, policies and audit evidence across frameworks.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software part of compliance tooling is a glorified checklist with file attachments and due dates, and yes, an agent can build that before dinner. The part you are actually buying is the mapping of a framework to concrete controls, kept current, plus connectors that pull evidence out of your cloud, identity provider and ticket tracker so nobody has to screenshot anything. Then there is the part that is not software at all: an auditor who accepts the output and a trust page that a prospect's security reviewer will read without flinching. A homegrown tracker gets you organized, which is genuinely useful, but it does not get you a report. If the goal is passing an audit or unblocking enterprise deals, the DIY build is a personal to do list wearing a compliance costume.
coreLoopDIY: A local control register where you define controls, attach evidence files with expiry dates, and get a readiness dashboard plus a Markdown export for your auditor.
requirements: Node 20 and a local machine or small VPS
Your own control list, since framework text is licensed and not something you should scrape
Manual evidence collection, or scripts you write per integration
An actual auditor if you need a real report
whatYouLose: Maintained framework to control mappings that change when the standards and interpretations do
Automated evidence collection from cloud, identity, HR and ticketing systems
Anything an auditor recognizes, including their workflow for requesting and reviewing samples
A hosted trust page and prefilled security questionnaire answers for sales
Alerts and ownership nudges that keep controls from quietly going stale
Someone to blame, and to call, when a reviewer disputes your evidence
moatNotes: Compliance tools sell certainty to a third party, not features to you. That third party has opinions about what it will accept.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody buys compliance software because the UI is delightful. They buy it because a customer's procurement team asked for a report, or a board asked for a status, and the tool shortens the distance between where the company is and a signed opinion from an auditor. The integrations matter because manual evidence collection is where internal programs die around month four, and the framework content matters because reading the standard yourself and guessing at control scope is how you fail a readiness review. A self-built tracker handles the organizing, which is the cheap half. The expensive half is the audit itself and the ongoing upkeep, and neither of those is a coding problem.
notes: The tracker is a weekend build; the audit is not. The moat is maintained framework mappings, evidence integrations, and an auditor who will sign off on whatever the tool spits out.
prompt:
Build a local-first compliance control register called Register. Single user, runs on my machine, no cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/register.db
- Drizzle for schema and migrations
- Evidence files stored on disk under ./data/evidence, never in the database
- Zod for all form validation

Data model:
- Control: id, code, title, description, owner, category, status (not-started | in-progress | implemented | not-applicable), reviewFrequencyDays, lastReviewedAt, notes
- Evidence: id, controlId, filename, originalName, mimeType, capturedAt, expiresAt, note
- Task: id, controlId nullable, title, dueDate, done

Features that are in scope:
- CRUD for controls, with a table view filterable by status, owner and category
- Control detail page: edit fields, upload evidence via drag and drop, list evidence with age and expiry state
- Readiness dashboard: counts by status, controls with no evidence, evidence expiring in the next 30 days, controls overdue for review based on reviewFrequencyDays
- Import and export controls as CSV so I can paste in my own control list
- One click export of a Markdown audit packet: every control, its status, owner, review date, and a list of attached evidence filenames
- Seed script that creates an empty database and about ten generic example controls I wrote myself, clearly labeled as examples

Explicitly out of scope, do not build or stub:
- Any framework text, control library, or crosswalk copied from SOC 2, ISO 27001 or similar, those are licensed
- Integrations with AWS, Google Workspace, Okta, Jira or anything else
- Multi user, roles, SSO, auth of any kind
- A public trust page or questionnaire autofill
- Email or Slack notifications, surface everything in the dashboard instead

Engineering notes:
- Any secrets go in .env with a committed .env.example, though this build should need none
- npm run seed, npm run dev, npm run build must all work from a clean clone
- Include a README that says plainly: this is an organizer, not an audit, and an auditor may not accept its output
- Write a handful of vitest tests for the overdue and expiring date logic, skip the rest
